crossCuttingFindings.finding: This repo has TWO scenario schemas. src/scenario/schema.js is a newer, separate engine (0..1 normalized coordinates, interaction kinds point/path/selection/sequence/place) that does NOT match what these drafts describe. The drafts' own stated type list (choice/multi/explain/position/sequence) instead matches src/one-on-one/experimentalBankCore.js's QUESTION_TYPES exactly -- that is the real target schema for this whole task, confirmed by cross-referencing every renderNotes uncertainty against it.

THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT SCHEMA FINDING IN THIS TASK. A real scenario object has exactly ONE 'setup' (actors + puck), shared by every question authored against that scenarioId -- confirmed against experimentalBankCore.js (no per-question setup override exists) and every real scene inspected in src/one-on-one/experimental-bank/. This directly resolves curriculum-gap-plan.json's own gap #7 uncertainty ('needs an engineering spike... to confirm whether a two-freeze scene is representable') in the negative: no, it is not representable as one scenario with a moved actor on a later question. BOTH of this set's paired baseline/hypothetical drafts (draft26-u11-cause-001 and draft26-u11-cause-002) violated this by rendering a moved defender for their 'q2' while calling the move hypothetical in the prompt -- self-contradictory, and also a direct violation of the family's own stated 'no claim of motion from a static pose' principle. Fixed in both pairs by pinning the hypothetical question's actor positions to the baseline and moving the stated change entirely into prompt text, exactly matching how the live bank's real 'Imagine.../Suppose...' questions already work.

The 'facing' field exists on every actor (required, Number.isFinite(a.facing)) but is a SINGLE static angle, never a two-state or animated value. This resolves the renderNotes uncertainty in both skating drafts (draft26-u15-skate-001-q1, draft26-u18-skate-002-q1): a turn or pivot cannot be rendered as two sequential poses; it must be narrated in briefing/cues text, with the render showing only the single POST-action facing.

The 'position' interaction type always moves a NAMED ACTOR to a coordinate/zone, scored by proximity, with basis schema-locked to 'coaching' (never objectively 'scene'-graded). It has no concept of an actor-independent static landmark region. draft26-u7-vocab-002-q1's premise ('tap the faceoff circle nearest the net') cannot be expressed in this type at all -- resolved by changing its type to 'choice', matching the working pattern from its paired draft.

Every scenario requires >=1 actor (with a resolvable focusActorId) and a puck object (owned by a skater, or loose with on-ice coordinates) UNCONDITIONALLY -- there is no 'no actors needed' path. Both U7 vocabulary drafts originally specified illustrativeActors:{} on the theory that a pure-landmark scene needs no players; this is not schema-valid. Fixed by adding one inert actor + puck to each, without changing either question's substance.

validateExperimentalBank requires 6-10 questions per real scenario, spanning at least 4 of the 5 supported types. Every one of these 10 drafts is a single question on its own scenarioId (except the two intentionally-paired cause-and-effect scenarios, which have 2 each). None of the four lesson briefs states that more questions were intended per scene, but the SCHEMA structurally requires far more before any of these could be admitted as real scenarios. This task does not manufacture 5-9 additional questions per scene to close that gap (that would be exactly the 'generating volume' the assignment says to avoid) -- it is recorded here as an explicit, unresolved authoring requirement that applies uniformly to all 10 drafts, not fabricated content.

Unlike the newer scenario-engine (which has an explicit rinkFrame.attackingDirection concept), the live one-on-one schema has NO dedicated field for which end a team attacks -- real scenes convey it only in prose (e.g., u11.json's briefing: 'Navy is in Navy's defensive zone... Navy defends the nearby net'). Every 'net'/'goal-side' reference in these revisions follows that same prose convention and is flagged as illustrative, not independently engine-verified, consistent with how Task A's own geometry-verification.json handled the identical limitation ('Navy attacks the +x end per the briefing').

optionAnalysis.option: Gold 1, now open through the middle
optionAnalysis.plausibleBecause: It is the marked-correct answer and matches the scene's stated intent: the turn buys separation away from F1's committed side.
optionAnalysis.whyItWorks: Gold1 sits ~8.5m of lateral ice away from F1's band (y=-3 vs F1's y=-11.5), and F1 is currently 6.02m off the direct YOU-Gold1 line (perpendicular, clamped at YOU's own position) -- there is no live coverage on that lane at this instant.
optionAnalysis.whenAlternativeWouldWork: If F1 had committed toward the middle instead of the boards before the turn, Gold1 (not Gold2) would be the exposed teammate and this answer would flip.

optionAnalysis.option: Gold 2, still in the same near-boards band as F1
optionAnalysis.plausibleBecause: Gold2 is a real, named teammate in a plausible passing position, not a joke or filler option.
optionAnalysis.whyItFails: F1 sits within 0.5m of Gold2's lateral band (near-boards, y around -11), so even though F1 is not literally ON the Gold2 lane at this instant either (also ~6.02m perpendicular off it), F1 can close that gap far faster than the ~8.5m gap to Gold1's band. This is a recovery-speed argument, not a 'lane already blocked' claim -- worth a qualified reviewer's confirmation that this reads correctly to a coach's eye, since the static engine cannot render recovery speed directly.
optionAnalysis.whenThisWouldWork: If F1 had already turned upfield and lost outside leverage on the boards entirely (e.g., beaten wide), Gold2 could become the better read instead.

optionAnalysis.option: Neither -- F1's position already threatens both lanes equally
optionAnalysis.plausibleBecause: Both lanes are geometrically ~6.0m off F1's current position, so a learner doing the arithmetic naively could conclude they are equal.
optionAnalysis.whyItFails: Equal perpendicular distance to a line is not the same as equal THREAT -- lateral band proximity (F1 essentially shares Gold2's band, 8.5m from Gold1's) is what actually differentiates the two options.
optionAnalysis.distractorPatternNote: The ORIGINAL wording of this option ('Neither, F1 recovers immediately') was revised. The original asserted a specific future outcome (F1's recovery) that a static freeze cannot show -- exactly the 'no claim of motion from a static pose' violation this audit is required to catch. The revised wording above states a checkable CURRENT-POSITION claim instead (equal current distance to both lanes), which is false for the reason given, without assuming any future motion.

A defender cannot close a 6m gap in two steps. REVISED wording above ('closes hard and gets between YOU and Gold1, cutting off that lane entirely') states the outcome without a specific, geometrically-implausible distance claim.
geometryAudit.hypotheticalMotionCheck: This is the exact case the audit is designed to catch: the ORIGINAL draft rendered F1 in a moved position while ALSO describing it as hypothetical ('Suppose...') in the prompt -- self-contradictory, since a moved render is not hypothetical, it is asserted. schemaValidation.renderNotesResolved: Original renderNotes asked: "Needs confirming how the 'explain' type's grading/acceptable-answer mechanism works in the current engine before finalizing the accepted-answer list." RESOLVED, and this is the single most important schema finding in this whole set: 'explain' questions have NO accepted-answer or grading mechanism at all. Per experimentalBankCore.js's reviewResponse(), the 'keyed' check (objective, scene-matched grading) only applies to types choice/multi/sequence with an 'answer' array -- 'explain' is never in that set, so reviewResponse always returns matched=null and a fixed generic heading ('A coaching suggestion'). The 'explanation' field is ALWAYS shown verbatim after any response, regardless of what the player typed -- it is fixed coaching text, not a comparison target. The original draft's plan to author 'an exact acceptable-answer set... against the explain type's actual grading rubric' describes something that does not exist to author against.
